one_liner: Header-only C++14 order-preserving trie for in-memory indexes. Beats STX B+-tree, ART and Masstree on string-key lookups, scans and memory.
what_it_does: HOT (Height Optimized Trie) is an ordered main-memory index from the SIGMOD'18 paper, meant as a secondary index over tuples you store yourself. It ships two class templates with the same API: HOTSingleThreaded<Value, KeyExtractor>, which has insert, upsert, lookup, remove, find, lower_bound, upper_bound, scan and const iterators, and HOTRowex<Value, KeyExtractor>, a concurrent version that has no remove. Each entry is at most 8 bytes and only 63 bits are usable, typically a tuple id or a pointer. The key is recomputed from that value through the KeyExtractor functor. Lookups return an OptionalValue rather than an iterator, so this is not a std::map-style container.
how_it_is_fast: It is a binary Patricia trie whose nodes are grouped into compound nodes of at most k=32 entries. Each node's span, meaning how many key bits it looks at, is chosen from the data so that the overall tree height is as small as possible, which keeps fanout high even for sparse string keys. Inside a node, the discriminative bit positions are stored as a single or multi byte mask, and the matching bits of the search key are gathered with one BMI2 PEXT. The result is compared against all of the node's 8/16/32-bit 'sparse partial keys' at once with AVX2 and/cmpeq/movemask, and the last match wins. Inserts rebuild partial keys with PDEP into copy-on-write nodes. Nodes come in 9 physical layouts, the node type is encoded in the low bits of each child pointer, and the first 4 cache lines of each node are prefetched. On the paper's string data sets the mean leaf depth is up to 68% lower than ART's.
when_to_use: Read-mostly in-memory ordered indexes on variable-length string keys of 255 bytes or less, such as URLs or emails. Paper workload C (50M keys): 1.3 vs 0.9 Mops/s for Masstree on URLs, and 1.5 vs 1.2 on emails.
Short range scans over string keys. On workload E (95% scans of up to 100 entries) over URLs, HOT ran 0.6 Mops/s against 0.2 for the STX B+-tree and ART and 0.1 for Masstree.

Memory-bound indexes. For 50M keys the paper measured 11.4-14.4 bytes/key: 0.53-0.67 GB against 1.26 GB for the STX B+-tree, 1.09-1.64 GB for ART and 1.53-5.05 GB for Masstree (all figures include 0.37 GB of raw tuple ids). HOT was also smaller than the raw URL and email key bytes.
Skewed or compound 8-byte keys, such as the yago triples: lookups ran 4.1 vs 2.4 Mops/s for ART.
Concurrent insert and lookup without deletes on Intel x86-64 Linux. HOTRowex readers never take locks, and the paper shows near-linear scaling to 10 cores (mean lookup speedup 9.96x, insert 9.00x).
when_not_to_use: Uniformly random 64-bit integer keys. Figure 8 shows lookups only ~6% ahead of ART (5.3 vs 5.0 Mops/s), and ART inserts 50% faster (3.9 vs 2.6 Mops/s).
Point lookups where you don't need key order. In issue #3, one user measured HOT at 82 ns/find and 236 ns/insert against Folly F14 at 27/31 ns, on ~570K short strings on a Xeon E-2278G.
Workloads that need concurrent deletes (HOTRowex has no remove), keys longer than 255 bytes, binary keys with zero bytes, or an index that owns its keys and values the way std::map does.

CPUs other than Intel Haswell or newer. AVX2, BMI2 and LZCNT are required. PEXT is slow on AMD Zen 1/2 (issue #8), and an ARM port using SIMDe ran 'very poor' (issue #10). MSVC and Windows are not supported as written.
Anything that needs upkeep. The code has been frozen since March 2018, nine issues from 2019-2024 have no maintainer reply, and the bundled build breaks on current toolchains.

integration.form: header-only (copy libs/idx/content-helpers, libs/hot/commons, libs/hot/single-threaded and/or libs/hot/rowex; CMake INTERFACE targets are also provided)
integration.dependencies: HOTSingleThreaded needs nothing outside the repo headers. HOTRowex needs Intel TBB (enumerable_thread_specific for epoch reclamation), and the README recommends tcmalloc. The repo's own build also pulls TBB 2018, boost-cmake 1.66 and Boost.Hana (for benchmarks and tests) as git submodules.
integration.min_toolchain: C++14, CMake 2.8+. The paper used GCC 7.2. On GCC 8+ the bundled benchmark framework fails to compile under -std=c++14 because of Boost.Hana constexpr lambdas (issues #1, #7). The code uses GCC attributes and glibc's __bswap_64.
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2, BMI2 and LZCNT (Haswell or newer); build with -march=haswell or native. Only Linux is documented. There is an optional USEAVX512 CMake flag. No ARM or other non-x86 support.
integration.thread_safety: HOTSingleThreaded is not thread-safe. All of its instances also share one unsynchronized function-static MemoryPool, so even separate trees on separate threads race. HOTRowex uses ROWEX: lookups and scans are wait-free and lock-free, and writers lock only the affected nodes (bottom-up) and restart when validation fails. Freed nodes go through a process-wide epoch-based reclamation singleton.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false — this is not a B-tree or std::map replacement. It indexes values of 8 bytes or less (63 usable bits) whose keys are re-derived through a KeyExtractor. lookup returns an OptionalValue, iterators are const-only, and the concurrent version cannot delete.

gotchas: The trie stores only your 63-bit value (tid or pointer), not the key. Every lookup ends by dereferencing the value through KeyExtractor and running a full compare (strcmp for strings), so the key memory must stay alive and unchanged while it is indexed.

C-string keys are capped at 255 bytes because bit offsets are uint8 (issue #6). KeyUtilities.hpp silently truncates longer keys to 255 bytes with strncpy/std::min instead of rejecting them, and every operation copies the key into a 255-byte fixed array.

There is no allocator hook. Nodes are allocated with posix_memalign (the single-threaded version adds a static free-list pool), a failed allocation throws std::bad_alloc, and inserts and deletes use an unchecked fixed 64-entry std::array traversal stack. The paper says HOT's worst-case height has not yet been proven.

Builds break out of the box. The pinned boost-cmake submodule commit can't be checked out (issue #2) and its Boost download URL returns 403 (issue #3). Without BMI/LZCNT target flags, GCC fails with 'inlining failed ... _tzcnt_u32' (issue #4).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick HOT over ART (ARTSynchronized or rafaelkallis/adaptive-radix-tree) when keys are strings or skewed and index memory matters. Stay with ART for uniformly random integer keys and insert-heavy loads, where HOT's own paper has ART inserting 50% faster at near-equal lookup speed. The learned-index siblings (RadixSpline, RMI, PLEX, fast64, PGM-index) report results on fixed-width integer key sets, while HOT needs no training and has its largest wins on variable-length strings.
verified_claims_summary: In the SIGMOD'18 paper, 50M keys (url, email, yago, random 63-bit integers) were loaded and then 100M uniform YCSB-style operations were run single-threaded on an Intel i7-6700 with GCC 7.2 (no flags stated). Workload C lookups ran 1.3/1.5/4.1/5.3 Mops/s against the best rival's 0.9 (Masstree), 1.2 (Masstree), 2.4 (ART) and 5.0 (ART), per the Figure 8 labels. So the text's 'at least 25% higher' holds for url, email and yago but not for integers (~6%). The '200% higher' is workload E on URLs (0.6 vs 0.2 Mops/s for the STX B+-tree and ART). The STX B+-tree baseline uses 256-byte nodes and resolves string keys through tuple ids, which helps explain its low string throughput.
status_note: Abandoned since 2018-03-26 with no active fork, and the code for the extended TODS 2022 'Height Optimized Tries' version (DOI 10.1145/3506692) was never released (issue #9). It is ISC-licensed and header-only, so vendoring the core headers is feasible, but expect to fix the build yourself; GCC 7.2 on Linux x86-64 is the last toolchain documented to work.
